newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi-backed Kurdish leader smells victory.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi-backed Kurdish leader smells victory.

text.p: Massoud Barzani, head of the Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), vowed on Monday to oust his long-standing rival from the city of Sulaimaniya, leaving his peshmerga fighters in control of northern Iraq.

Barzani, the Kurdish leader aligned with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, met politburo members under the trees of Dukan after his militia seized the town from Jalal Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
Little now stands in his path to the city of Sulaimaniya, the last big Iraqi base for Talabani's weary fighters.

"It is up to Mr Talabani whether he is willing to admit defeat or not. If he does we will go to elections to rebuild the government," said the 50-year-old Barzani, clad in traditional dress that included his trademark headband.
On Monday the KDP raced across 70 km (45 miles) of PUK-held lands to make its way to Dukan. Come Tuesday, Barzani said, his forces would advance another 70 km to Sulaimaniya.
"The people are asking us to go to Sulaimaniya. I don't see any reason not to go but we won't go today. So you can say that our plan is to go to Sulaimaniya," he told reporters.
Barzani and Talabani have been feuding off and on for three decades. After the 1991 Gulf War they appeared reconciled and each side took 50 seats in a regional Kurdish government election in 1992.
But the disputes continued -- most notably over the KDP's lock on "taxes" collected from Turkish border traders and the PUK's seizure of Arbil, capital of the largely Kurdish north.
Before the latest fighting Barzani controlled the northwest, while Talabani held the centre and southeast.
The KDP began overrunning PUK-held areas nine days ago when, backed by Iraq, it took Arbil from the PUK. Since then the KDP says it has been acting without Iraq.

Barzani said he was surprised how swiftly his men had overtaken the PUK, starting with the village of Degala and the city of Koi Sanjaq on Sunday and ending on Monday with the Dukan Dam, site of a hydroelectric plant crucial to the region.

The PUK could stand for election, he said but added: "The PUK should know that they are not the equivalent of the KDP. We'll ask the parliament and the government to work for elections by the end of the year."
Thousands of Kurds fled the fighting for the Iranian border in anything that moved -- cars, minibuses and even a bulldozer.
Was Barzani worried about pushing too far for fear of an Iranian response?
"We have no problems with the Iranians if they do not interfere with us. They should not interfere with this fighting," he said.
